domain: International Law / Security Studies / Constitutional Interpretation
topic_summary: Analysis of Article 51 of the UN Charter as a contested kernel where different interpretive communities read the same textual commitment ('inherent right of individual or collective self-defence') as generating structurally different constraints on the legitimate use of force. The narrow reading constrains force to responses to actual/imminent armed attacks by states; the expansive reading permits preemptive/preventive force against non-state actors and emerging threats.

key_entities: UN Charter Article 51 (textual kernel: 'inherent right of individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs')
UN Security Council (constitutional authority to determine threats to peace; Article 39-42 enforcement monopoly)
International Court of Justice (judicial interpretive authority; Nicaragua case precedent)
Powerful military states (US, Russia, China, Israel—actors with capacity for unilateral force projection)
Weaker/target states (populations in regions subject to preventive strikes; Global South states)
Non-state armed groups (Al-Qaeda, ISIS—actors whose threat profile destabilizes state-centric framework)
key_tensions: Collective security primacy vs sovereign security discretion (Security Council authorization requirement vs unilateral self-defense claims)
State-centric framework vs transnational threat reality (armed attack by 'state' vs terrorist network harbored in failed state)
key_claims: Narrow reading: Article 51 self-defense is triggered only by an actual or imminent armed attack by a state attributable under international law
Expansive reading: Article 51 inherent right permits preemptive force against non-state actors when host state is unwilling/unable to act
Security Council: Article 51 is an exception to Article 2(4) prohibition on force, not a standalone authorization
Powerful states post-9/11: Transnational terrorism creates gaps in Charter framework that self-defense must fill
key_mechanisms: Security Council veto system (P5 monopoly on enforcement authorization; deadlock permits unilateral action in practice)
Customary international law evolution (state practice + opinio juris can modify Charter interpretation over time)
Imminence doctrine (Caroline test: necessity must be instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice of means, no moment for deliberation)
key_absences: Absence of enforcement mechanism for Charter violations (no sanction for expansive reading violations beyond reputational cost)
Absence of agreed definition of 'armed attack' threshold (accumulation-of-events doctrine vs single-incident requirement)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Article 51 UN Charter text as fixed reference point for legitimate self-defense claims—all parties invoke it as the authoritative source, but read it differently
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy contested between ICJ judicial interpretation (narrow reading's institutional anchor) and state practice/custom (expansive reading's evolutionary anchor). Security Council authorization serves as procedural override but is structurally paralyzed by P5 veto.

readings.commitment: Self-defense is constrained to responses to an actual or imminent armed attack by a state attributable under international law
readings.authority_grounding: ICJ judicial interpretation (Nicaragua case, Oil Platforms case); collective security primacy via Security Council Article 39 authority
readings.expected_structural_delta: High constraint on unilateral force; non-state actor threats do not trigger Article 51 unless attributable to host state; beneficiaries are weaker states and multilateral institutions whose authority is preserved; victims are powerful states whose strategic freedom is constrained

readings.commitment: Self-defense extends to preemptive or preventive uses of force against non-state actors or emerging threats when necessity is demonstrated
readings.authority_grounding: State practice (US, Israel, Russia); sovereign security discretion; Bush Doctrine post-9/11; customary law evolution claim
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low constraint on unilateral force; necessity determination is self-judged by acting state; beneficiaries are militarily capable states and defense sectors; victims are target-region populations and multilateral veto authority

readings.commitment: Self-defense is triggered when a non-state actor attack originates from a host state that is unwilling or unable to suppress the threat, creating a hybrid constraint
readings.authority_grounding: Hybrid: accepts ICJ state-attribution requirement but loosens it via inability/unwillingness proxy; US legal position post-Syria strikes; pragmatic accommodation
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate constraint—requires non-state actor attack to have occurred (not purely preventive) but permits unilateral response when host state fails to act; beneficiaries are intervening states with counterterrorism mandates; victims are host states whose sovereignty is bypassed

axiom_contradictions.basis: Narrow reading's foundational axiom is that Charter Article 2(4) prohibition on force is the rule and Article 51 is a narrow exception requiring Security Council authorization or actual armed attack; expansive reading's axiom is that inherent sovereign right of self-defense predates the Charter and permits unilateral judgment of necessity. No single coherent framework can hold both: accepting Security Council primacy as binding requires rejecting unilateral necessity discretion, and vice versa.

axes.structural_delta: Self-defense constrained to actual/imminent armed attacks by states; non-state threats require Security Council authorization
axes.primary_observable: ICJ case law (Nicaragua, Oil Platforms); state invocations citing Article 51 + Security Council reporting under Article 51 duty
axes.selection_reason: Core reading with high epsilon; institutionally anchored in ICJ jurisprudence; structurally distinct beneficiary/victim pair

axes.structural_delta: Self-defense permits preemptive/preventive force against non-state threats; necessity is self-judged by acting state
axes.primary_observable: State practice (Bush Doctrine invocations, Israeli preventive strikes, Russian Georgia/Ukraine justifications); defense expenditure patterns in anticipatory capabilities
axes.selection_reason: Axiom-contradictory to narrow reading; captures post-9/11 drift in state practice; structurally opposite epsilon

axes.structural_delta: Self-defense triggered by non-state attack when host state cannot/will not suppress threat; hybrid constraint bypassing strict state-attribution
axes.primary_observable: US legal memoranda (Syria strikes 2017-18); NATO invocations post-Afghanistan; state practice distinguishing inability from unwillingness
axes.selection_reason: Pragmatic middle position; captures real-world accommodation mechanism; structurally distinct from binary narrow/expansive opposition

axes.structural_delta: P5 veto power creates structural deadlock on force authorization, incentivizing unilateral Article 51 claims
axes.primary_observable: Security Council resolution veto frequency on use-of-force matters; gap between Article 51 letters filed and Security Council authorizations
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: upstream mountain feeding all readings; structural bottleneck is context for kernel contest but not itself a reading

axes.structural_delta: Repeated expansive invocations + acquiescence may modify Article 51 constraint via customary international law evolution
axes.primary_observable: State practice frequency; opinio juris evidence in legal memoranda; third-party state responses (protest vs acquiescence)
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: mechanism of drift rather than a reading; captured implicitly in expansive reading's authority grounding

deferred_axes.structural_delta: P5 veto creates authorization bottleneck incentivizing unilateral claims
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Upstream structural constraint feeding all readings; provides context but not itself a reading of Article 51

deferred_axes.structural_delta: State practice may modify Article 51 constraint via customary law
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Mechanism of drift rather than distinct reading; captured in expansive reading's authority grounding

omegas.description: ICJ lacks enforcement power—narrow reading's authority is judicial but not coercive. If powerful states ignore ICJ rulings, does narrow reading become a Piton (atrophied norm) rather than a Rope (functioning constraint)?
omegas.source: Absence Inventory (no enforcement mechanism for Charter violations)

omegas.description: Absence of agreed 'armed attack' threshold—accumulation-of-events vs single-incident. Does this ambiguity structurally advantage expansive reading by creating interpretive space for lowering the trigger?
omegas.source: Absence Inventory (no agreed definition of armed attack)

omegas.description: Does Article 51 apply to cyber attacks? Neither reading explicitly addresses non-kinetic threats. Omission may require fourth reading (cyber-equivalence doctrine) for structural completeness.

Three-reading selection may underweight emerging 'humanitarian intervention as self-defense' hybrid (R2P claims invoking Article 51). Deferred but structurally relevant to Global South victim analysis.
omegas.source: Selection budget constraint + Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan)

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition is clean: three readings are structurally distinct (different epsilon bins, different beneficiary/victim pairs), axiom contradiction between narrow and expansive is validated (Security Council primacy vs sovereign discretion cannot coexist), and unable/unwilling doctrine occupies genuine middle ground. Security Council paralysis and customary evolution are correctly deferred as mechanisms rather than readings.
